title: Why Alaska Has This Weird Strip of Coast (6 Judges Decided)
hook: Why does Alaska have a long thin strip hanging off its side?

scenes.heading: Why the Panhandle?
scenes.subheading: A courtroom drama in three exhibits
scenes.narration: Why does Alaska have a long, thin strip hanging off its side? <short pause> Today we're treating it like a trial. Three exhibits, six judges, and one very awkward verdict.
scenes.delivery: curious, intriguing, like opening a case file
scenes.caption: CASE FILE: ALASKA

scenes.narration: Look at Alaska on a globe and something's off. There's a big mainland up north, then a skinny ribbon of coast trailing down along British Columbia like a tail. Mapmakers call it the Panhandle. It exists because of an 1825 treaty. And a 1903 argument decided how far inland it reached.
scenes.caption: THE ODD TAIL

scenes.narration: Our story starts with Russia, which ran Alaska as a fur-trading colony from Sitka. By 1867, Russia was short of money, the fur trade was fading, and it feared it couldn't defend such a faraway place against Britain. So it sold the lot to the United States.
scenes.caption: RUSSIA SELLS, 1867

scenes.label: per acre, the price of Alaska in 1867
scenes.narration: The price was seven point two million dollars. That works out to roughly two cents an acre. <short pause> Cheap, sure. But America had bought a border that was written down but never surveyed, and ambiguous.
scenes.delivery: wry and amused, then a hint of foreshadowing
scenes.caption: THE BARGAIN

scenes.heading: Exhibit A
scenes.narration: So, Exhibit A. The treaty that was supposed to settle everything.
scenes.caption: EXHIBIT A

scenes.narration: Back in 1825, Russia and Britain had agreed on a line. It started at the south end of Prince of Wales Island, then followed the mountain crests along the coast. If the mountains were too far inland, the line would sit a set distance from the shore instead.
scenes.caption: THE 1825 LINE

scenes.label: the maximum distance from the coast, ten marine leagues
scenes.narration: That set distance was ten marine leagues. It's about fifty-five kilometres. Simple enough on paper.
scenes.caption: TEN LEAGUES

scenes.narration: But this coast is shredded with deep fjords, and the mountains aren't a tidy wall. Did the line jump across the mouth of each inlet, or follow the water's edge up inside? Nobody knew. And for decades it hardly mattered.
scenes.caption: FJORDS & FUZZ

scenes.heading: Exhibit B
scenes.narration: Then came Exhibit B. <short pause> Gold.
scenes.delivery: low, dramatic, a beat of silence before the word
scenes.caption: EXHIBIT B

scenes.narration: In August 1896, gold turned up in a creek in Canada's Klondike. Once the news hit Seattle in July 1897, tens of thousands headed north. The most popular way in was by ship to the head of a fjord, then over the mountain passes on foot.
scenes.caption: KLONDIKE RUSH

scenes.narration: Those towns were Skagway and Dyea, at the head of Lynn Canal's northern arm. Tents, saloons and mud, within months. And here's the catch: whoever owned that fjord's head controlled the doorway to the goldfields.
scenes.caption: SKAGWAY & DYEA

scenes.label: of supplies each person had to bring over the pass, roughly a ton
scenes.narration: And the Canadian Mounties required about a year's supplies, roughly a ton. <breath> Climbing a frozen pass, load after load, week after week. That's why the route mattered so much.
scenes.caption: A TON OF GEAR

scenes.narration: Suddenly the vague treaty mattered. Canada argued the line should cut across the fjords, which would put the head of Lynn Canal in Canadian hands, and give the Klondike its own seaport. America said the line followed the windings of the coast, up inside every inlet, so the fjords, and Skagway, were American.
scenes.delivery: tense, laying out two sides fairly
scenes.caption: TWO CLAIMS

scenes.narration: Let's line the dates up. A loose treaty in 1825. A sale in 1867. Gold in 1896. A stampede in 1898. And by 1903, someone had to settle it.
scenes.caption: HOW IT BUILT UP

scenes.heading: Exhibit C
scenes.narration: Which brings us to Exhibit C. The tribunal.
scenes.caption: EXHIBIT C

scenes.narration: In early 1903, the US and Britain, which still spoke for Canada abroad, agreed to let six judges decide. They'd meet in London. Canada had pushed for a neutral umpire; the US refused, so the compromise was an evenly split panel.
scenes.delivery: even, procedural, with a flicker of irony
scenes.caption: LONDON, 1903

scenes.narration: Here's the panel. Three Americans, two Canadians, and one British judge: Lord Alverstone, the Lord Chief Justice. The treaty promised 'impartial jurists', but the American picks were politicians. <short pause> And look at those bars. Everything hinged on one man in the middle.
scenes.caption: THE SIX JUDGES

scenes.narration: And President Theodore Roosevelt wasn't being subtle. In 1902 he sent more troops to Alaska, and privately warned he'd enforce the US line if the tribunal failed. Britain, meanwhile, wanted a warm friendship with a rising America.
scenes.caption: BIG STICK

scenes.narration: The last puzzle was four small islands at the mouth of the Portland Canal. Alverstone split them: two to each country. Many historians see that as a compromise to look fair, while he sided with the Americans on the big question.
scenes.caption: ISLAND SPLIT

events.label: Lynn Canal goes to the US
Two Canadian judges refuse to sign

scenes.narration: The award was announced on October 20th. The US won the heads of the fjords, so Skagway and Dyea stayed American. And the two Canadian judges refused to sign. They called the ruling a political deal, not a legal one.
scenes.delivery: solemn, then sharper at the refusal
scenes.caption: THE VERDICT

scenes.narration: That verdict locked in the shape on your map. A long ribbon of American coast walling northwestern British Columbia and the Yukon off from the Pacific. The Klondike had no Canadian seaport, and still has none today.
scenes.caption: THE SHAPE LOCKED IN

scenes.label: roughly how long the Panhandle is
scenes.narration: A strip roughly eight hundred kilometres long, because a clause written in 1825 left the status of the fjords unclear.
scenes.caption: THE TAIL

scenes.narration: In Canada, the sting lasted. Many felt Britain had traded away their interests to please Washington. Historians think it helped push Canadians toward running their own diplomacy; Ottawa created a Department of External Affairs in 1909.
scenes.delivery: warm, reflective, with a note of empathy
scenes.caption: CANADA'S LESSON

scenes.narration: What if the ruling had gone the other way? Probably Skagway would be Canadian, and the Panhandle would be much narrower, cut off from the interior. The map you grew up with came down to six people in a London room.
scenes.caption: WHAT IF?

scenes.heading: A Line Drawn in a Room
scenes.subheading: Next time you see a strange border, ask who argued about it
scenes.narration: So that's the Panhandle. Not mountains. Not nature. Just a vague sentence, a gold rush, and a verdict. <short pause> Borders are stories. Go find the next one.
scenes.caption: CASE CLOSED

description:
In 1903 a six-judge tribunal in London settled a long-running argument over Alaska's border, deciding how far inland the long coastal strip we call the Panhandle reached and keeping the heads of the fjords American. This video explains how a vague 1825 treaty, the Klondike Gold Rush and a politically charged verdict produced one of North America's oddest shapes.

Sources: Norman Penlington, "The Alaska Boundary Dispute: A Critical Reappraisal" (1972); Pierre Berton, "Klondike: The Last Great Gold Rush, 1896-1899"; U.S. National Park Service, Klondike Gold Rush National Historical Park; U.S. Department of State, Office of the Historian.

Animation and narration are AI-assisted; script reviewed by a human.
